title: DFS in Lisbon: Real Streets, Deep-First Chaos ⚡
description: Watch DFS explore Lisbon’s Alfama street grid like a stack-driven detective—choosing one path deep before backtracking. This reel visualizes how DFS traversal behavior changes routes compared to other graph search strategies.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps ⚡ What happens when DFS picks one street and dives deep into Alfama intersections? 

In this visualization, we convert real streets into a graph: intersections become nodes, road connections become edges. Then DFS (Depth First Search) runs with a stack/recursion rule—go as deep as possible, then backtrack when a dead end or visited node appears. 

Technical breakdown (what you’re seeing):
• LIFO behavior drives the “deep-first” path
• A visited set prevents infinite loops on cyclic road graphs
• Backtracking reveals why DFS may reach the goal late even if a shorter route exists

Takeaway: DFS is great for reachability and exploring structure, but it’s not guaranteed to find the shortest path on street networks.

Debate question: Should route-finding on real cities prioritize “deep discovery” (DFS) or “shortest-first” (BFS/Dijkstra)—and why?
